content.title: Does the resurrection really matter?
content.summary: Christ rose bodily. Our forgiveness and hope depend on it.

answer.text: Yes. Jesus actually rose from the dead, bodily and gloriously. Paul says that without his resurrection faith would be futile and we would remain in our sins. The resurrection is God's saving act in history, not a metaphor for the disciples keeping Jesus' ideals alive.

reasoning.text: Paul passes on the message of Christ's death for sins, burial, resurrection and appearances.
Luke presents Jesus showing his body and eating with his disciples.
Christ's resurrection is the beginning and guarantee of his people's resurrection.

conclusion.text: The Christian hope rests in the risen Christ himself, not merely in the psychological value of believing a resurrection story.

sections.text: First Corinthians 15 reports appearances to named people and to a large group. It is Paul's account of witnesses; we do not possess 500 separate statements in that passage. A strong case should describe the evidence we actually have.
sections.title: Use the testimony accurately

sections.text: Read the accounts, examine objections and explain why the testimony is credible. Do not turn an argument into a substitute for God's authority or the Spirit's work. Christianity's supernatural claims cannot be removed while leaving its gospel intact.
sections.title: Historical reasoning serves the Word

content.objection: Could the disciples simply have meant that Jesus' influence survived?

reply.text: That does not fit the claim of the texts: the tomb is empty, Jesus appears, and Paul ties his resurrection to our future bodily resurrection.

limit.text: A summary cannot settle every historical objection. Distinguish Scripture's testimony, your explanation of it and additional reconstructions that may remain uncertain.

prompt.text: Could we read the resurrection testimony and ask what difference it makes if Christ really rose?

passages.note: The risen Jesus among his disciples
